evidence: Word-by-word. SOURCE (the approved working-copy script's first question): "Where are my body parts?". DRAFT: "Let's see if I can find my body parts.". Kept: the object ("my body parts"), the speaker ("I", the reader saying the script to themselves, as in the source) and the step itself, locating one's body parts, which the four questions after it (feet, position in the chair, breathing, place in the room) then carry out. Changed: a bare question becomes a self-invitation. That brings in two things his line does not have. "Let's" is the idiom said to oneself: the finder is still "I" ("if I can find"), so no other party is added and nobody else does anything. "See if I can" makes the finding an attempt where the question took it as answerable; that is a gentler register of the same step, not a claim, not a condition on anything the reader must do, not a number or a person, and the script's own next lines speak in the same "if" voice ("If you’re there little one", "If there is something we need to do"). I checked both and accept them as register, within what the_change names: Emulate's sentence, its "Lets" typo fixed, for the first question, and nothing else. The_change claims nothing put back, and nothing of his is owed. In context the paragraph reads right (a statement, then his four questions, which are unchanged). One problem found: the typo fix. The "Let's" in DRAFT.txt and CONTEXT.txt line 5 has a straight apostrophe, but every other contraction in the section is curly (you’re twice, I’m three times, didn’t, in CONTEXT.txt lines 7 and 9), so it would be the one straight apostrophe among curly ones, an artifact of the fix. It should be "Let’s". Tell rows, judged on the literal draft in its section. I judge it justified: the four questions are his approved script and unchanged, a grounding script is a sequence of short prompts said in order, and the draft shortens the run (the first of five questions becomes a statement) and adds none. T07 considered ("Let's see if I can" as simulated casualness): not present; it is the first step of a script the reader says, not filler between beats of an argument, and the lines around it are in the same voice. T19 considered: not present; it is the script's own first line, not a sentence to the reader about the script (the lead-in above it is that). T22 not present (self-talk, no reassurance); T26 not present ("my body" repeats only in his unchanged questions); T15 not present (the structure changes, not just words); C02 not present ("if I can" pins "Let's" to "I", so there is no referent the reader has not seen); C03 not present (a line the reader says, not a fact about Joel); T11, T20, T25, T29 and the other rows absent in a one-sentence opener.
